analysis.title: Oil chart set, 4Q26 edition
key_insights: Global observed oil inventories fell by a combined 371 million barrels from March to September, and UBS says lower inventories should support prices given the negative correlation between oil prices and inventories.
OECD commercial inventories have moved sideways, helped by the release of strategic oil inventories. About 1 billion barrels of OECD strategic reserves remain, but not all of them can be used.
The latest coordinated SPR release planned 400mb, with around 330mb effectively released. It helped tame the price increase earlier this year.
Oil prices first outpaced the drop in OECD commercial inventories, then overcorrected against the historical pattern. UBS says prices are now back at the historical relationship.
US gasoline and distillate inventories are low, driven by high domestic and foreign demand. Refined product prices trade at a high premium to crude.
The futures curve is in steep backwardation and Dated Brent trades above the front-month Brent future. UBS reads both as signs of a tight market.
Oil on water is rising because more oil is leaving the Middle East, ship-to-ship transfers are increasing, and transit routes are longer to bypass choke points.
Dirty VLCC tanker freight rates have soared. UBS cites the Middle East conflict risk premium, ship-to-ship transfers, sanctions, higher fuel costs and longer routes.
US petroleum exports are at a record, though higher freight costs and lower US inventories are likely curbing the pace of exports.

Lower Chinese imports left more oil for the rest of the world. With domestic inventories falling, China has returned to the market, and preliminary October data point to imports of around 10 million barrels per day.
US oil demand has been weaker than last year in recent months, likely because of high pump prices. TSA throughput and European flight activity remain supported.
Indian oil consumption rose 3.4% y/y to 19.259 million metric tons in September, with diesel +5.6% and gasoline +8.0%. Pump prices there are controlled.
UBS does not expect oil demand to peak anytime soon. It expects slower growth over the next decade, with emerging markets as the driver. Demand grew about 1.2mbpd per year over the last 20 years.

The conflict cut global oil production by more than 10mbpd, followed by a recovery in recent months. Middle East crude exports have almost recovered, but Gulf loadings stay volatile because of regular strikes on energy infrastructure and vessels.
More than 20 million barrels per day of crude and refined products were exported via the Strait of Hormuz before the conflict started.
The oil market currently has no OPEC spare capacity, and unplanned outages stand close to record levels. UBS calls the Middle East disruption the largest supply disruption in history.
Higher prices have supported US drilling, with rigs and frac-spreads recovering, but US production growth has been modest so far. UBS expects higher growth that is not yet visible.

Brazilian output has surged to new highs and Guyanese output keeps rising, but UBS expects more modest growth going forward. Major project start-ups are expected over 2025-27, with a slowdown over 2028-30.
Russian crude production is not growing. Refinery attacks have made more crude available for export and weighed on refined product exports.
Speculative net length in WTI and Brent futures and options has risen modestly in recent months and remains light.

sector_views.rationale: The report argues that low inventories, steep backwardation, no spare capacity and record supply disruption support oil prices. It states no formal sector rating.

macro_indicators.indicator: Global observed oil inventories change, March to September
macro_indicators.interpretation: Inventory draws are negatively correlated with oil prices and should support prices.
Transport fuel demand is supported by controlled pump prices.
China is returning to the market as domestic inventories fall, which removes a source of spare barrels for the rest of the world.
The release tamed the price increase earlier this year. About 1 billion barrels remain, not all usable.

macro_indicators.indicator: Global oil production loss from the conflict
macro_indicators.interpretation: Production has since recovered in recent months.

risk_factors: Further strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure and vessels could keep supply volatile.
No OPEC spare capacity leaves little buffer against outages.
High pump prices have weakened US oil demand versus last year.
Higher freight costs and lower US inventories may curb US exports.
Strategic reserves cannot all be used, limiting further SPR releases.
US production growth could accelerate in response to higher prices, which is not yet visible.
charts_described: Page 3 and 4 charts plot a negative correlation between oil prices and global observed oil inventories, with end-September marked.
Page 8 charts show OECD SPR sales monthly in million barrels and OECD SPR oil inventories in billion barrels.
Page 28 charts show US oil rigs and frac-spread recovering and US crude production growth slowing.
vol_and_positioning: Speculative accounts have modestly increased net length in WTI (NYMEX) and Brent (ICE) futures and options in recent months, and positioning remains light.
The oil futures curve is in steep backwardation and Dated Brent trades above the front-month Brent future.
geopolitical: Middle East conflict has caused the largest supply disruption in history and cut global oil production by more than 10mbpd.
Regular strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure and vessels keep daily crude loadings volatile.
More than 20 million barrels per day moved through the Strait of Hormuz before the conflict, and longer routes now bypass choke points.
Sanctions and a Middle East risk premium have lifted tanker freight rates.
Attacks on Russian refineries have made more crude available for export and weighed on refined product exports.
